title: The king who preached on a mountain
sum: Abijah, Rehoboam's son, reigns three years. Kings gives him eight lines and a poor verdict (1 Kings 15:1–8). Chronicles gives him one great day. Facing Jeroboam's army, twice the size of his own, he climbs Mount Zemaraim and preaches to the north: the kingdom belongs to David's house by a covenant of salt, Jeroboam is a rebel, his priests are hirelings of golden calves, and Judah still keeps the LORD's worship. "Don't make war on the LORD."

Jeroboam answers with an ambush. Surrounded, Judah cries out, the priests blow the trumpets, the men raise the war cry, and God strikes Israel down. Judah wins "because they had leaned on the LORD." Abijah takes Bethel, Jeroboam never recovers, and Abijah grows strong.
readings: Read as history

A border war between Judah and Israel in Benjamin is likely; Kings mentions "war between Abijam and Jeroboam" (1 Kings 15:7), and the capture of Bethel would explain the later border at Ramah (16:1). The vast numbers and the polished speech are best read as the Chronicler's way of telling it.
Read as theology

The chapter is the Chronicler's charter for the divided kingdom. The north has two sins, rejecting David's house and the Aaronic priesthood, and Judah's strength is its faithfulness to both. Yet the speech calls the northerners "Israelites" and invites them back: the door is open.

views.H: Traditional readers take Abijah's speech and victory as history that Kings passed over, noting that Kings itself mentions the war. Kings' bad verdict on Abijam and Chronicles' praise can both be true: he sinned, yet trusted God in this battle.
views.C: Critical scholars see a model battle shaped by the Chronicler: a sermon, a ritual of trumpets and shouting, and a miraculous victory. Some think a real border clash and the capture of Bethel lie behind it.
views.S: Compare 1 Kings 15:1–8. Chronicles keeps the date, the length of reign and "there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam," but drops Kings' verdict that "his heart was not whole" and his mother's name (Micaiah here, not Maacah). All of 13:3–21 is Chronicles' own.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition was harder on Abijah than Chronicles: the Talmud and midrash say he was punished for insulting Jeroboam publicly and for mutilating the slain, which is how some read "The LORD struck him" (13:20) as a blow on Abijah himself.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in Abijah's speech the claims that the true worship of God is tied to God's chosen king and priest, which the New Testament applies to Christ as son of David and high priest (Hebrews 7–8).

deep.b:
Kings and Chronicles agree on the facts they share and disagree on the man. Kings sums him up in the formula for a bad king: "He walked in all the sins his father had committed before him" (1 Kings 15:3), and keeps David's line alive only "because of David." Chronicles gives no verdict at all. It lets Abijah speak and fight, and the result is the verdict: God was with him. This is one of the clearest places where Chronicles' own material changes a reader's impression of a king.

Both books may be partial. Kings judges each king by his worship at the high places and tolerance of idols; Chronicles here judges by his loyalty to the Temple and to David's house in one decisive moment.

echoes: 1 Kings 15:1–8; 1 Kings 12:25–33; Numbers 10:9; Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 11:13–17; 2 Chronicles 30:6–9

settings.to: Jeroboam and all Israel, drawn up for battle
settings.when: In Abijah's war with Jeroboam, about 913 BC
settings.why: A sermon before battle: the kingdom belongs to David's sons by a 'covenant of salt'; Jeroboam rebelled; his priests serve golden calves; Judah keeps the LORD's priests and daily worship. 'Israelites, don't make war on the LORD.' Kings gives Abijah only a poor verdict (1 Kings 15:3). Chronicles gives him the book's clearest statement of its view of the north: wrong king, wrong priests. Yet he calls them 'Israelites' and pleads with them. For readers facing Samaria's rival claims, it said that true Israel worships at Jerusalem, and that the door is open.
views: Abijah's own words
Traditional readers: a real speech recorded in 'the commentary of the prophet Iddo' (13:22).
A Chronicler's sermon
Most critical scholars, following von Rad, read it as one of the Chronicler's 'Levitical sermons' written for his own day.
Aimed at Samaria
Some see an attack on the Samaritan community of the Chronicler's time; others, with Williamson, read an appeal to return.

title: Asa and the million-man army
sum: Asa begins well. He removes foreign altars, high places, standing stones and Asherah poles, and he tells Judah to seek the LORD and keep the law. The land is quiet for ten years, and he builds fortified towns: "We sought him, and he gave us rest."

Then Zerah the Cushite invades with "a thousand thousands" and three hundred chariots. At Mareshah Asa prays a short prayer of complete dependence: for the LORD it makes no difference whether the side is strong or weak; "we lean on you." The LORD strikes the Cushites, and Judah pursues them to Gerar and returns with herds and camels.
readings: Read as history

A raid from the southwest is plausible after Shishak's invasion (12:2–9). Whether Zerah led an Egyptian army, a Nubian force, or a tribe of the Negev is debated (see 14:9). No Egyptian or other record mentions him.
Read as a lesson

The chapter sets out Chronicles' pattern in its clearest form: seeking God brings rest, building and victory. It prepares for the reversal in chapter 16, where Asa will lean on Aram instead of the LORD.

views.H: Traditional readers accept Zerah's invasion as history and see in it a reward for Asa's reforms, as Chronicles says.
views.C: Critical scholars note the rounded pattern (reform, rest, building, army, victory) and the enormous numbers, and many doubt the details while allowing a historical border clash in the southwest.
views.S: Kings has only the summary of Asa's reforms (1 Kings 15:11–15). Chronicles' chapter 14, apart from 14:1–2, is its own. Kings says Asa left the high places; Chronicles here says he removed them (see 15:17).
views.J: Rabbinic readers valued Asa's prayer as a model of trust. Some midrashim praise his courage; others criticize him for later relying on Aram and on physicians.
views.X: Christians have used Asa's prayer ("we lean on you, and in your name we have come") as a model of confident prayer in weakness, compared with Paul's "when I am weak, then I am strong" (2 Corinthians 12:10).

settings.to: The people of Judah
settings.when: In the ten quiet years at the start of his reign
settings.why: 'We sought the LORD our God. We sought him, and he gave us rest on all sides.' Asa ties peace to seeking God and uses it to build. For readers in a quiet time under Persia, it said that rest was a gift to use well.

settings.to: The LORD his God
settings.when: Facing Zerah the Cushite's huge army in the Zephathah Valley
settings.why: 'For you there is no difference in helping, whether the side is great or has no strength... we lean on you.' A short prayer of trust, told only in Chronicles. The victory that follows shows readers, a small people, that numbers do not decide the outcome.

title: A covenant to seek the LORD
sum: The prophet Azariah son of Oded meets Asa after the victory with a sermon on one theme: "The LORD is with you as long as you are with him. Seek him, and he will let you find him. Leave him, and he will leave you." He recalls a time of chaos when Israel had no true God, no teaching priest and no law, and how they found God in their distress.

Asa takes heart. He removes idols, repairs the altar, and gathers Judah, Benjamin and many northerners in the fifteenth year, in the third month. They enter a covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart, on pain of death, and swear it with shouts and trumpets. Asa removes the queen mother Maacah (his grandmother, on the usual reading), burns her Asherah image and brings gifts to the Temple. There is no war until the thirty-fifth year.
readings: Read as covenant renewal

The scene follows the pattern of Israel's covenant ceremonies: a prophetic word, removal of idols, sacrifice, oath and joy, perhaps at the Feast of Weeks (15:10). Similar renewals come under Jehoiada (23:16), Hezekiah (29:10) and Josiah (34:31–32).
Read as a sermon to the Chronicler's readers

Azariah's speech borrows language from Zechariah and Jeremiah. Many scholars hear it addressed to the Chronicler's own community: in uncertain times, seek God and your work will have its reward (15:7).

views.H: Traditional readers take Azariah as a real prophet and the covenant as a historical event in Asa's fifteenth year, after the victory of chapter 14.
views.C: Critical scholars note the prophetic quotations and the Chronicler's vocabulary in the speech and see a composition that interprets Asa's reign; they debate whether a real reform lies behind it.
views.S: Only 15:16–18 runs parallel to Kings (1 Kings 15:13–15), and the Plain uses the same English there. Chronicles adds "crushed it" and "from Israel." The rest of the chapter is Chronicles' own.
views.J: Jewish readers have linked the third-month assembly with Shavuot, the festival of the covenant at Sinai, and 15:3 ("no God of truth, no priest who taught, no law") was read in rabbinic literature as a description of the exile.
views.X: Christian readers have quoted 15:2 as a statement of the conditions of fellowship with God, and some have discussed the death penalty of 15:13 as a mark of the old covenant's form of community, not to be copied by the church.

deep.b: 15:19 and 16:1 date the end of peace and Baasha's attack to Asa's thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth years. By Kings' figures Baasha was dead by Asa's twenty-sixth year (1 Kings 15:33; 16:8). The explanations are: counting from the division of the kingdom (Seder Olam, Rashi, Thiele), which gives Asa's fifteenth and sixteenth years and fits 15:10; a copying error in the numbers; or a deliberate shaping of Asa's reign in Chronicles into long faithfulness and a late fall (see the note on 15:19 and the topic "Dating the Kings").

echoes: Deuteronomy 4:29; Jeremiah 29:13; Zechariah 8:10; Jeremiah 31:16; Hosea 3:4–5; 1 Kings 15:13–15; Deuteronomy 13:6–10

settings.by: Azariah son of Oded, with the Spirit of God on him
settings.to: Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin
settings.when: As Asa returned from the victory over Zerah
settings.why: 'The LORD is with you as long as you are with him. Seek him, and he will let you find him. Leave him, and he will leave you.' He recalls a time without God, priest or law, when Israel turned and found him, and ends, 'Be strong... your work will have its reward.' The sermon pushes Asa to reform. Many scholars hear it as speaking directly to the Chronicler's readers, whose times were uncertain and whose work on the Temple and the law needed courage.
views: A prophet to Asa
Traditional readers: Azariah's words to the king, preserved by the Chronicler.
A sermon for the readers

Many critical scholars: the speech borrows from Zechariah and Jeremiah and was shaped as a sermon for the post-exilic community. The time when 'Israel had no God of truth' may recall the judges or the exile.

settings.what: Asa's covenant to seek the LORD
settings.to: The LORD; binding all Judah and Benjamin and the northerners who had come over
settings.when: Asa's fifteenth year, in the third month, at Jerusalem
settings.why: The people swear to seek the LORD with all their heart and soul, on pain of death for anyone who would not. The oath binds every Israelite, man or woman, great or small, and it ends in joy and rest. For readers it was a model of covenant renewal like their own (Nehemiah 10), and its harsh clause shows how seriously the book takes turning away.

title: The king who leaned on Aram
sum: In his thirty-sixth year Asa faces Baasha of Israel, who fortifies Ramah to choke Jerusalem. Asa empties the treasuries of the Temple and palace to buy Ben-hadad of Damascus, who attacks northern Israel. Baasha withdraws, and Asa uses his stones to fortify Geba and Mizpah. In Kings the story ends there, a success.

Chronicles adds Hanani the seer. Asa leaned on the king of Aram instead of on the LORD, who had given him the Cushites; "the LORD's eyes roam all over the earth" to strengthen the wholehearted; "you have acted like a fool," and there will be wars. Asa puts the prophet in the stocks and oppresses some of the people. In his thirty-ninth year he falls sick in his feet, and does not seek the LORD but the healers. He dies in his forty-first year and is buried with spices and a great fire.
readings: Read as a moral tragedy

Asa's story turns on the word "lean" (13:18; 14:11; 16:7–8). A king who once trusted God against a million men now trusts silver and Damascus, then doctors. The decline is told without hiding the honor he still received at death.
Read beside Kings

Kings treats the treaty as shrewd politics. Chronicles reads the same facts as unbelief, and its additions (Hanani, the prison, the illness without seeking God) are the clearest example of how Chronicles turns a report into a judgment.

views.H: Traditional readers take Hanani's rebuke and Asa's late decline as history Kings omitted, and Asa as a warning that a good beginning does not guarantee a good end.
views.C: Critical scholars see the Chronicler's doctrine of retribution: Kings' report of a foot disease late in life needed a cause, and Chronicles supplied it in the treaty and the persecution of a prophet.
views.S: 16:1–6 copies 1 Kings 15:17–22 closely, and the Plain uses the same English there. Note what Chronicles changes: no "payment" (bribe), no "all the silver," "Abel-maim" and "store towns" for "Abel-beth-maacah" and "Kinnereth." 16:7–10 and the details of 16:12–14 are Chronicles' own.
views.J: The Talmud discusses Asa's seeking of physicians and affirms that the Torah permits medicine (Bava Kamma 85a); Asa's fault is understood as abandoning prayer, not consulting doctors.
views.X: Christian preachers have used 16:9 widely ("the eyes of the LORD run to and fro") as a promise of God's help to the wholehearted, and Asa as an example of faith that weakens with success.

echoes: 1 Kings 15:16–24; Zechariah 4:10; 1 Samuel 13:13; Jeremiah 20:2; Exodus 15:26; Ben Sira 38:1–15; Jeremiah 34:5

settings.to: Ben-hadad king of Aram in Damascus
settings.when: When Baasha of Israel fortified Ramah, Asa's thirty-sixth year
settings.why: The same scene as 1 Kings 15:18–19: Asa pays Aram, with Temple silver, to break its treaty with Israel. Kings reports it without comment. Chronicles sets it against Asa's earlier faith and has a seer condemn it at once (16:7–9). Readers learn that buying a foreign king's help is leaning on the wrong arm. Chronicles' date (Asa's thirty-sixth year, 16:1) does not fit Kings, where Baasha died in Asa's twenty-sixth year (1 Kings 16:6–8), and scholars explain it in different ways.

settings.to: Asa king of Judah
settings.when: Right after the treaty with Aram
settings.why: 'Because you leaned on the king of Aram and did not lean on the LORD.' He reminds Asa of the victory over the Cushites and says 'the LORD's eyes roam all over the earth' to support those whose hearts are whole. The rebuke was meant to bring Asa back; he jailed the seer instead. For readers who lived among empires, it said where real help comes from.

title: Jehoshaphat sends out teachers
sum: Jehoshaphat succeeds Asa and strengthens Judah against Israel. The LORD is with him because he follows the early ways of David and seeks his father's God, not the Baals. All Judah brings him tribute, his heart "rises high in the LORD's ways," and he removes high places and Asherah poles.

In his third year he sends officials, Levites and priests through the towns of Judah with the scroll of the LORD's law to teach the people. The dread of the LORD keeps the neighbors at peace; Philistines and Arabs bring tribute. Jehoshaphat builds forts and store towns, and five commanders lead an army of over a million.
readings: Read as history

A strong, prosperous Judah under Jehoshaphat fits what Kings suggests: he was Ahab's ally rather than his vassal (1 Kings 22:4; 2 Kings 3:7). The teaching mission has no parallel in Kings and is debated (see 17:7).
Read as the ideal king

The chapter is a portrait: seeking God, teaching the law, removing idols, receiving tribute, building and defending. It echoes the law of the king in Deuteronomy, who keeps a copy of the law and reads it (Deuteronomy 17:18–20).

views.H: Traditional readers accept the teaching mission as one of Jehoshaphat's reforms, with his judicial reform (19:4–11), true to his name "the LORD judges."
views.C: Many critical scholars think the teaching Levites reflect the Persian period (Nehemiah 8), and the vast army the Chronicler's way of showing blessing.
views.S: Kings has nothing parallel here except the note that Jehoshaphat succeeded Asa (1 Kings 15:24; 22:41–43). Chronicles' four chapters on Jehoshaphat are mostly its own.
views.J: Jewish tradition honored Jehoshaphat as a righteous king and a teacher of Torah; the Talmud praises him for rising from his throne to greet scholars (Makkot 24a).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in 17:7–9 an example of teaching Scripture to the people, cited in support of education and preaching ministries.

echoes: Deuteronomy 17:18–20; Deuteronomy 33:10; Nehemiah 8:7–9; 2 Chronicles 19:4–11; Malachi 2:7; 1 Kings 22:41–43

settings.what: Jehoshaphat's teaching mission with the scroll of the law
settings.by: Jehoshaphat, through five officials, nine Levites and two priests
settings.to: The people in all the towns of Judah
settings.when: Jehoshaphat's third year
settings.why: Teachers travel with 'the scroll of the LORD's law' so that the people learn it in their own towns. The law binds every Judean, and here the king takes responsibility for teaching it. Told only in Chronicles, it looks like the teaching of Ezra and the Levites (Nehemiah 8:7–8) in the readers' own day, and gives that work royal roots.

title: Micaiah and the lying spirit
sum: Rich and honored, Jehoshaphat marries into Ahab's family and visits Samaria, where Ahab feasts him and lures him into a war for Ramoth-gilead. Jehoshaphat agrees but asks for the LORD's word. Four hundred prophets say, "Go up." Jehoshaphat asks for another, and Micaiah son of Imlah is fetched. He first mocks the court prophets' answer, then tells his vision: Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd, and the LORD in his council sending a lying spirit into the prophets' mouths to lure Ahab to his death.

Zedekiah strikes him, and Ahab sends him to prison until he returns "in peace." In the battle Ahab disguises himself and leaves Jehoshaphat in royal robes. The Aramean chariots close in on Jehoshaphat; he cries out, "the LORD came to his aid; God coaxed them away from him." A random arrow strikes Ahab, who dies at sunset.
readings: Read as prophecy

The chapter asks how to tell true from false prophecy. Four hundred agree; one man stands alone, refuses to speak anything but what God says, and is proved right. Micaiah's test is Deuteronomy's: a word that does not come true was not from the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:21–22).
Read as Chronicles' story of Jehoshaphat
Copied almost word for word from 1 Kings 22, the chapter becomes in Chronicles a story about Judah's king: lured into a bad alliance, saved by prayer, and then rebuked (19:1–3).

views.H: Traditional readers take the account as history recorded in both Kings and Chronicles, and the heavenly council as a true prophetic vision.
views.C: Critical scholars treat 1 Kings 22 as a prophetic story of uncertain historical setting (the king is unnamed in much of it) and see Chronicles' few changes as theological.
views.S: This is the longest straight parallel in this part of Chronicles. Where the Hebrew is the same, the Plain uses the site's wording of 1 Kings 22. Chronicles adds 18:1–2 and "The LORD came to his aid; God coaxed them away from him" (18:31), and stops at Ahab's death, leaving out the dogs and Elijah's word.
views.J: The Talmud asks why Jehoshaphat distrusted four hundred prophets and answers that true prophets never speak with exactly the same words (Sanhedrin 89a). The "spirit" of 18:20 is identified there with the spirit of Naboth.
views.X: Christian interpreters have discussed the lying spirit at length as a case of God using evil for judgment (compare 2 Thessalonians 2:11), and Micaiah as a model of costly faithfulness.

deep.title: Claude's theory: who came back "in peace"?
deep.b: This is my reading, not an established view. The word shalom frames the story. Micaiah sees the LORD say, "Let each of them go home in peace" (18:16). Ahab says he will stay until he can "come back in peace" (18:26), and Chronicles changes Kings' verb here to shuvi, "my return," so that Ahab's words match Micaiah's reply exactly. Micaiah answers, "If you really do come back in peace, the LORD has not spoken through me" (18:27). Kings never uses the word again. Chronicles' first added sentence after the battle is that Jehoshaphat "came back in peace to his house" (19:1). I think the Chronicler added this to show both halves of Micaiah's word fulfilled: the shepherd of Israel falls, and the sheep, including Judah's king, go home in peace. Commentators have noted the link between 18:27 and 19:1; the reading of 18:16 as fulfilled in Jehoshaphat is my own extension.

echoes: 1 Kings 22:1–40; Deuteronomy 18:21–22; Isaiah 6:1–8; Job 1:6–12; Matthew 9:36; 2 Thessalonians 2:11

settings.what: Jehoshaphat's pledge and the four hundred prophets
settings.by: Ahab and Jehoshaphat; Zedekiah son of Kenaanah and the prophets
settings.to: Each other; the two kings at the gate of Samaria
settings.when: Before the attack on Ramoth-gilead, about 853 BC
settings.why: The same scene as 1 Kings 22:4–12. Jehoshaphat pledges 'I am one with you' and asks for the LORD's word; the court prophets promise victory with one voice. Kings tells the story to judge Ahab. Chronicles tells it about Jehoshaphat, a good king who made a bad alliance by marriage (18:1). Readers are warned against ties with those who do not seek the LORD.

settings.to: Ahab king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah, sitting on their thrones
settings.when: The same day, at the gate of Samaria
settings.why: Micaiah first mocks the court's answer, then sees Israel scattered like sheep and the LORD's council sending a lying spirit into Ahab's prophets. He is struck and jailed. The vision is read in different ways (see the views). For the Chronicler's readers it was a lesson in telling true prophets from flattering ones, and in why Jehoshaphat should have listened.
views: The LORD rules even over false prophecy
Many readers: God's council sends the lying spirit, so even the court prophets serve his judgment on Ahab.
A figure for the prophets' own deception
Others read the scene as a picture, not a report: Micaiah shows the king that his prophets are deceived, and leaves him free to listen. See the 1 Kings 22 card for more views.

settings.to: The LORD
settings.when: When Aram's chariot commanders closed in on him, taking him for the king of Israel
settings.why: 'Jehoshaphat cried out. The LORD came to his aid; God coaxed them away from him.' Kings says only that he cried out (1 Kings 22:32). Chronicles makes the cry a prayer that God answers. Even in a battle he should not have joined, the king who seeks the LORD is heard.

title: Judges who judge for God
sum: Jehoshaphat comes home in peace, and Jehu son of Hanani meets him: "Is it the wicked you should be helping?" Wrath is on him, but good has been found in him too. The king responds by going out himself from Beersheba to Ephraim's hills, turning the people back to the LORD.

He appoints judges in every fortified town and charges them: you judge not for people but for the LORD; let the dread of the LORD be on you, for with him there is no crookedness, favoritism or bribery. In Jerusalem he sets up a court of Levites, priests and family heads, under Amariah the head priest for the LORD's matters and Zebadiah for the king's.
readings: Read as history
The reform fits Jehoshaphat's name and his strong reign. Albright and others argued it is authentic; others see the Chronicler drawing on Deuteronomy 16–17.
Read as teaching on justice

The charge to the judges (19:6–7, 9–10) is one of the Bible's fullest statements on the ethics of judging: judges act for God, must fear him, must be impartial and incorruptible, and must teach and warn so that guilt does not spread.

views.H: Traditional readers take the reform as history, a fulfillment of Deuteronomy's commands by a king who also taught the law (17:7–9).
views.C: Critical scholars debate whether the court system reflects the ninth century or the Persian period, with its division of priestly and royal spheres (19:11).
views.S: Nothing in this chapter is in Kings. Chronicles uses the prophet Jehu son of Hanani, known from Kings (1 Kings 16:1–7), to judge the alliance Kings records without comment (1 Kings 22:44).
views.J: Jewish tradition used Jehoshaphat's charge, with Deuteronomy 16:18–20, in teaching on the duties of judges; the phrase "for the LORD... in the matter of judgment" was read as meaning God sits with the judges (compare Psalm 82:1).
views.X: Christian writers have applied 19:6–7 to all who hold authority, and the verses have been cited in discussions of the ethics of judges and magistrates.

echoes: Deuteronomy 1:16–17; Deuteronomy 10:17; Deuteronomy 16:18–20; Deuteronomy 17:8–13; Exodus 18:13–26; Psalm 82:1–4; 1 Kings 16:1–7

settings.what: Jehu son of Hanani rebukes Jehoshaphat
settings.by: Jehu son of Hanani the visionary
settings.to: Jehoshaphat, returning to Jerusalem
settings.when: After Ahab's death at Ramoth-gilead
settings.why: 'Is it the wicked you should be helping?... But good things have been found in you.' The rebuke names both the sin and the good. It shows readers a God who weighs a king's whole heart, and it leads into Jehoshaphat's reforms.

settings.what: Jehoshaphat's charge to the town judges
settings.to: The judges he set in each fortified town of Judah
settings.when: After he went out among the people from Beersheba to Ephraim
settings.why: 'It is not for people that you judge, but for the LORD.' The charge binds local judges to fear God, show no favor and take no bribe, as Deuteronomy 16:18–20 requires. It answers the problem of crooked justice in the towns. For readers, whose courts were run by elders, priests and Levites under Persian law, it set justice under God's eye.

settings.what: Jehoshaphat's charge to the Jerusalem court
settings.to: The Levites, priests and family heads appointed as a court in Jerusalem
settings.when: At the same time
settings.why: A higher court for hard cases sent up from the towns, as in Deuteronomy 17:8–13. Amariah the head priest is over 'every matter of the LORD,' Zebadiah the leader of Judah over 'every matter of the king.' The judges must warn their brothers so guilt does not spread. The split between religious and royal cases matched the readers' world, where the high priest and the Persian governor shared authority.
views: A real reform
Albright and others: a real judicial reform under Jehoshaphat, whose name means 'the LORD judges.'
The Chronicler's reading of Deuteronomy 16–17
Knoppers: the account shows how the Chronicler reworked Deuteronomy's court laws for his own picture of Jehoshaphat.
A later system read back
Others: the Chronicler describes the courts of his own day.

title: The battle won by singing
sum: Moab, Ammon and the Meunites cross from beyond the Dead Sea to En-gedi. Jehoshaphat is afraid, calls a fast, and prays before all Judah in the Temple court: God rules every kingdom, gave this land to Abraham's offspring, and promised to hear prayer at this house. "What we should do, we do not know. Our eyes are on you." The Spirit comes on Jahaziel, a Levite singer: "The battle does not belong to you. It belongs to God... Take your stand, stand still, and watch the LORD save you."

At dawn Jehoshaphat urges, "Hold firm to the LORD your God, and you will be held firm," and sends singers ahead of the army: "Give thanks to the LORD, for his loyal love is forever." As they sing, the LORD sets ambushes; the invaders destroy each other. Judah spends three days gathering plunder and blesses the LORD in the Valley of Beracah, then returns to Jerusalem with harps, lyres and trumpets. The chapter closes with the summary of Jehoshaphat's reign and his failed shipping venture with Ahaziah.
readings: Read as history

A raid from Moab and Ammon by way of En-gedi is plausible, and Moab's king Mesha boasts of victories over Israel in these years. Some scholars think 2 Chronicles 20 retells the Moabite war of 2 Kings 3 in a new form; others think it preserves a separate local tradition from the Tekoa area.
Read as worship

The chapter is a liturgy: fast, assembly, lament, oracle, worship, procession, thanksgiving, return to the Temple. Its message to later readers, without a king or army, is that worship and trust are Israel's real defense.

views.H: Traditional readers take the victory as history, a miracle like those at the Sea and in Gideon's battle, and Jahaziel's oracle as true prophecy.
views.C: Critical scholars read the chapter as a model holy-war story, built from the exodus, Gideon and the psalms, and told for a community whose only weapon was worship. They debate its historical core.
views.S: Only 20:31–37 has a parallel (1 Kings 22:41–49). Chronicles drops Kings' "high places" sacrifices for a judgment on the heart (20:33), cites Jehu son of Hanani as its source (20:34), and turns Jehoshaphat's refusal of Ahaziah's help into a partnership condemned by a prophet (20:35–37).
views.J: Jewish tradition noted that the singers praised "his loyal love is forever" without "for he is good," because God takes no joy in the fall of the wicked (Babylonian Talmud Megillah 10b), a teaching also linked to the Sea of Reeds.
views.X: Christians often cite 20:15 and 20:21–22 in teaching on praise and spiritual warfare: worship is not a reward after victory but the way the victory comes.

deep.b: Both chapters tell of Jehoshaphat facing Moab with allies or against allies, in the south, with a prophet's word (Elisha; Jahaziel), and an enemy confused into destroying itself (2 Kings 3:21–24; 2 Chronicles 20:22–23). Some scholars (Noth among them) think Chronicles' story grew from a separate local memory; others that it reworks 2 Kings 3. Traditional readers see two different campaigns. The comparison shows how Chronicles tells holy war: no army moves, only singers.

echoes: Exodus 14:13–14; Exodus 15:1–21; Judges 7:22; 1 Samuel 17:47; Isaiah 7:9; Deuteronomy 2:4–19; Psalm 136:1; 2 Kings 3:4–27; 1 Kings 22:41–49

settings.what: Jehoshaphat's prayer in the Temple court
settings.to: The LORD, before the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem with their wives and children
settings.when: During a national fast, as Moab, Ammon and the Meunites came through En-gedi
settings.why: He calls on the God who rules every kingdom and recalls the gift of the land. He cites Solomon's promise that God would hear at this house (6:28–30), and ends, 'What we should do, we do not know. Our eyes are on you.' It is the clearest example of praying as 7:14 asks. For readers with no army, it was the prayer they could pray.

settings.by: Jahaziel son of Zechariah, a Levite singer of Asaph's line, with the Spirit of the LORD on him
settings.to: All Judah, the people of Jerusalem and King Jehoshaphat
settings.when: In the middle of the assembly, after the king's prayer
settings.why: 'The battle does not belong to you. It belongs to God... stand still, and watch the LORD save you.' The words echo Moses at the Red Sea (Exodus 14:13–14). The prophet is a Temple singer, which shows the honor Chronicles gives the Levites. For readers it said that worship, not weapons, was their defense.

settings.what: Jehoshaphat's charge and the singers' refrain
settings.by: Jehoshaphat; then the singers he appointed
settings.to: Judah and the people of Jerusalem going out to Tekoa; then the LORD
settings.when: Early the next morning
settings.why: 'Hold firm to the LORD your God, and you will be held firm. Hold firm to his prophets, and you will succeed,' a play on Isaiah 7:9. Singers lead the army: 'Give thanks to the LORD, for his loyal love is forever.' The battle is won as they sing. For readers, the scene made the Temple choir the front line of faith.

settings.by: Eliezer son of Dodavahu, from Mareshah
settings.to: Jehoshaphat
settings.when: After his partnership with Ahaziah of Israel to build ships
settings.why: 'Since you have partnered with Ahaziah, the LORD has broken apart your work.' Kings says only that the ships were wrecked (1 Kings 22:48–49). Chronicles gives a prophet's reason. Readers hear once more the warning against alliances with kings who do evil.

title: Jehoram and the letter from Elijah
sum: Jehoshaphat dies, and his firstborn Jehoram, married to Ahab's daughter, kills his six brothers and some officials. He walks in the road of Israel's kings. The LORD spares David's house for the covenant's sake, but Edom and Libnah revolt.

Then a letter comes from Elijah the prophet: because Jehoram has led Judah into unfaithfulness and killed brothers better than himself, the LORD will strike his people, his family and his goods, and he will die of a disease of the bowels. Philistines and Arabs raid Judah and carry off his wives and sons, all but the youngest. After two years of illness he dies in agony, unmourned, and is buried outside the royal tombs.
readings: Read as history
Kings confirms the revolts of Edom and Libnah and the marriage to Ahab's house (2 Kings 8:16–24). The fratricide, the raids and the illness are only in Chronicles.
Read as retribution

Chronicles shapes the reign as a precise reversal: the king who killed his brothers loses his sons; the king who loved Ahab's ways hears from Ahab's great prophet; the king who brought ruin dies without honor.

views.H: Traditional readers accept the letter as genuine, written by Elijah before his ascension or while still alive (see 21:12), and the judgments as history.
views.C: Critical scholars consider the letter a composition of the Chronicler in Elijah's name and the raids and illness as his explanation of Jehoram's misfortunes.
views.S: 21:1 and 21:5–10 follow 2 Kings 8:16–22 and 1 Kings 22:50, and the Plain uses the same English where the Hebrew is the same. Chronicles changes "Judah" to "David's house" (21:7), "Zair" to "with his commanders" (21:9), drops the army's flight, and adds the reason for Libnah's revolt (21:10).
views.J: Rabbinic chronology (Seder Olam) dates the letter after Elijah was taken up, and medieval commentators explained it as written in advance or sent from heaven.
views.X: Christian readers have discussed the letter in debates about Elijah's ascension and continuing role (Malachi 4:5; Matthew 17:3), and Jehoram's end with the deaths of later persecutors (Acts 12:23).

echoes: 2 Kings 8:16–24; 1 Kings 22:50; 2 Kings 2:1–12; 2 Kings 1:17; 2 Kings 3:11; Judges 9:5; Acts 12:23

settings.to: Jehoram king of Judah, Jehoshaphat's son, married to Ahab's daughter
settings.when: During Jehoram's reign, about 848–841 BC, after he killed his brothers
settings.why: The only word of Elijah in Chronicles, and the only letter from a prophet in the histories. It condemns Jehoram for walking in the ways of Ahab's house and killing brothers 'better than you,' and announces a blow on his people and a disease of the bowels. The north's great prophet is brought to judge a southern king who copied the north. For readers it showed that the same God judged both kingdoms, and that Judah was no safer for being Judah.
views: Written before his ascension
Some traditional readers: Elijah wrote it before he was taken up, foreseeing Jehoram's sins, or Jehoram's reign overlapped with his father's while Elijah still lived.
Sent after his ascension
Radak and others: the letter came after Elijah was taken up. Elijah revealed himself to a prophet and gave him the words.
The Chronicler's composition
Many critical scholars: the Chronicler wrote the letter in Elijah's name to give a prophetic reason for the king's end. 2 Kings 3:11 suggests Elijah was gone by Jehoshaphat's day.

title: Ahaziah, Jehu and Athaliah
sum: The people of Jerusalem crown Jehoram's youngest son Ahaziah, the only one left. His mother Athaliah and Ahab's family are his advisers "to his ruin." He joins Jehoram of Israel against Aram at Ramoth-gilead and visits him at Jezreel, where God has planned his downfall: Jehu, anointed to destroy Ahab's house, kills Judah's officials and Ahaziah's nephews, then finds Ahaziah hiding in Samaria and kills him. They bury him for his grandfather Jehoshaphat's sake.

Athaliah destroys the royal family and seizes the throne. But Jehoshabeath, King Jehoram's daughter and wife of Jehoiada the priest, steals the baby Joash from among the dying princes and hides him in the Temple for six years.
readings: Read as history

Kings tells the same events (2 Kings 8:25–29; 9:27–28; 11:1–3). Chronicles differs in Ahaziah's age (42, an error; see the variant), in his death, and in naming Jehoshabeath as Jehoiada's wife. The Tel Dan inscription may give Hazael's claim to have killed Ahaziah.
Read as the low point of the dynasty
God promised David a lamp for all time (21:7). By 22:12 that lamp is one hidden baby. The chapter shows the promise kept by a woman's courage and a priest's house.

views.H: Traditional readers harmonize the two accounts of Ahaziah's death and see God's preservation of Joash as the keeping of the covenant with David, preserving the line of the Messiah.
views.C: Critical scholars see Chronicles abbreviating Kings and retelling Ahaziah's death with its own theology (22:7). The Tel Dan inscription complicates both accounts.
views.S: Compare 2 Kings 8:25–29, 9:27–28 and 11:1–3. Chronicles uses "Jehoram," "Joram" and even "Azariah" as its Hebrew does (22:5–6), adds the advisers (22:3–5), reverses the order of the killings (22:8), and has him caught in Samaria and brought to Jehu, where Kings has him die at Megiddo (22:9).
views.J: Jewish tradition honored Jehoshabeath and Jehoiada for saving the line of David. Medieval Jewish commentators explained the forty-two years of 22:2 by counting them from the start of Omri's dynasty.
views.X: Christian readers have long seen in the rescue of Joash a link in the chain that leads to Jesus, son of David, and some compared Athaliah's massacre to Herod's (Matthew 2:16).

title: The priest crowns the king
sum: In the seventh year Jehoiada acts. He brings five commanders into a covenant, gathers the Levites and family heads from all Judah, and presents the king's son to the assembly in God's house: "He will reign, just as the LORD said of David's sons." On a Sabbath, with both shifts of priests and Levites present and armed with King David's spears and shields, they crown Joash, give him the testimony and anoint him. "Long live the king!"

Athaliah hears the noise, sees the king by his pillar and the singers leading praise, and cries "Conspiracy!" Jehoiada has her taken out and killed at the Horse Gate. He makes a covenant that the people will be the LORD's, the people tear down the house of Baal, and Jehoiada restores the priests' and Levites' duties "as the law of Moses has it written... by David's direction." Joash is enthroned, and the city has rest.
readings: Read as history
A palace coup led by the high priest, with the Temple guard, is told in both Kings and Chronicles. Kings' version, with foreign guards in the Temple, is generally thought closer to the event.
Read as the Chronicler's ideal

Chronicles retells the coup as a sacred assembly: Levites instead of mercenaries, holiness rules observed, music, covenant, and worship restored by Moses' law and David's order. For readers after the exile, with a high priest but no king, the picture of a priest preserving David's line mattered.

views.H: Traditional readers combine Kings and Chronicles: Carites and runners guarded the palace and outer areas, while the Levites guarded the Temple itself.
views.C: Critical scholars see the Chronicler revising Kings to fit the purity rules and Levitical roles of his own day.
views.S: Compare 2 Kings 11:4–20 closely; the Plain uses Kings' English where the Hebrew matches. Chronicles names the officers, replaces the Carites and runners with Levites and nobles, adds the singers, makes Jehoiada a party to the covenant, and adds the restoration of Temple service (23:18–19).
views.J: Jewish tradition honored Jehoiada as a righteous high priest; his burial among the kings (24:16) was taken as a sign of his greatness.
views.X: Christian readers have seen Jehoiada as a type of faithful priestly leadership that protects the royal line, and the coronation as a picture of the hidden king revealed.

settings.to: The whole assembly in God's house: the officers over the hundreds, the Levites from all Judah's towns and the heads of families
settings.when: The seventh year of Athaliah's rule, on a Sabbath at the change of the guard
settings.why: The same scene as 2 Kings 11:4–8, the secret crowning of the boy Joash. But where Kings has the royal guard, Chronicles has the Levites ring the king. It adds: 'Let no one come into the LORD's house except the priests and the Levites who serve.' The purpose changes. Kings shows David's line saved by soldiers; Chronicles shows it saved without breaking the Temple's holiness, a lesson for readers whose Temple was guarded by Levites.

settings.by: Jehoiada, his sons and the people
settings.to: Joash, crowned and given the testimony
settings.when: In the LORD's house, with the Levites around the king
settings.why: 'Long live the king!' The same scene as 2 Kings 11:12, but here Jehoiada and his sons anoint the king, and singers lead the praise (23:13). For readers with no king, it pictured David's line restored by priests and Levites within the Temple's holy order.

settings.to: Himself, all the people and the king
settings.when: After Athaliah was killed
settings.why: The same scene as 2 Kings 11:17, with one change. The priest makes the covenant 'between himself and all the people and the king.' So a priest stands where the LORD stands in Kings. For readers whose high priest was the leading Jew in Yehud, the covenant showed priestly leadership keeping the people faithful when there was no proper king.

settings.what: Jehoiada's order for the Temple service
settings.to: The Levite priests and the gatekeepers
settings.when: After the covenant and the removal of Baal's house
settings.why: Jehoiada puts the Temple back in the hands of the Levite priests, by David's divisions and the law of Moses, 'with joy and with song.' He sets gatekeepers to keep the unclean out. The rule restores the order of 1 Chronicles 23–26 after Athaliah. It is told only in Chronicles, and it matched the readers' own Temple order.

title: The Temple restored, the prophet stoned
sum: Joash reigns forty years and does right all the days of Jehoiada. He sets his heart on renewing the Temple. When the Levites are slow to collect, he reminds Jehoiada of Moses' tax for the tent of the testimony. A chest is placed at the Temple gate, the people give gladly, and the Temple is rebuilt and strengthened; leftover silver makes vessels. Jehoiada dies at a hundred and thirty and is buried among the kings.

Then the officials bow to the king, and he listens to them. Judah leaves the Temple for Asherah poles and idols. Prophets warn in vain. The Spirit clothes Zechariah son of Jehoiada, who rebukes them, and at the king's command he is stoned in the Temple court. Dying, he says, "May the LORD see it, and may he seek it out." Within a year a small Aramean army defeats Judah, and Joash's servants kill him in bed for the blood of Jehoiada's son. He is not buried with the kings.
readings: Read as history
Kings records the repair, Hazael's threat and the assassination (2 Kings 12). Chronicles adds the apostasy and Zechariah's murder, and gives a reason for the assassination that Kings lacks.
Read as a mirror

The chapter is built as two halves: Joash with Jehoiada (the Temple restored, honor) and Joash without him (the Temple abandoned, a priest's son killed in its court, dishonor). Jehoiada buried among the kings and Joash outside them seals the verdict.

views.H: Traditional readers accept Chronicles' fuller account, seeing Joash as a king whose goodness depended on his mentor, and Zechariah as a true martyr.
views.C: Critical scholars think the Chronicler explained Joash's violent end (and the Aramean defeat) as punishment for a sin he identified, perhaps using a separate tradition about Zechariah's murder.
views.S: Compare 2 Kings 12. Chronicles changes who collects (Levites), where the chest stands (outside), what the surplus buys (vessels), how the Aramean crisis ends (defeat, not tribute), and why Joash dies (Zechariah's blood). The killers' parents become an Ammonite and a Moabite mother.
views.J: Jewish tradition remembered Zechariah's murder as one of the worst crimes in Israel's history: seven sins in one act, and his blood seething in the Temple court until the Babylonians came (Jerusalem Talmud Taanit 4:5; Babylonian Talmud Gittin 57b; Lamentations Rabbah).
views.X: Jesus' words "from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah" (Luke 11:51; Matthew 23:35) are usually traced to this chapter. Christian readers contrast Zechariah's dying plea for justice with Jesus' and Stephen's prayers for forgiveness.

deep.h: Who is Zechariah son of Berechiah?
deep.b: Matthew's form of Jesus' saying names "Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar" (Matthew 23:35). The prophet Zechariah was "son of Berechiah, son of Iddo" (Zechariah 1:1), but no account of his murder exists. Explanations include: Matthew or an early scribe confused two Zechariahs; Jesus meant the priest of 2 Chronicles 24, and "Abel to Zechariah" spans the Hebrew Bible from Genesis to Chronicles in the order the Talmud gives (Bava Batra 14b), though the Aleppo and Leningrad codices put Chronicles first among the Writings; the reference is to Zechariah father of John the Baptist (Protevangelium of James 23–24, Origen); or Zechariah son of Bareis, murdered in the Temple in AD 68 (Josephus, Jewish War 4.334–344), on the view that the saying looks forward. Most commentators favor the first two combined (Davies and Allison).

deep.title: Claude's theory: Moses' tax and the LORD's burden
deep.b: This is my own reading. The chapter opens with Joash collecting the mas'at Mosheh, "Moses' tax" (24:6, 9), a word from the root nasa, "to lift, carry," which also gives "silver by the load" (17:11) and loads of plunder (20:25). It closes with "the great oracle (massa) against him" (24:27), from the same root. I suggest the Chronicler meant the echo: the king who raised Moses' tax for the house ends with the LORD's "burden" raised against him for the blood shed in that house. The double sense of massa as oracle and burden is widely discussed (compare Jeremiah 23:33–38), and the note on 24:6 points to the shared root. What I add is the suggestion that the frame is deliberate. I have not checked whether a commentator has argued this.
deep.refs: 2 Chronicles 24:6; 2 Chronicles 24:9; 2 Chronicles 24:27; Jeremiah 23:33–38; 2 Chronicles 17:11; 2 Chronicles 20:25

echoes: 2 Kings 12:1–21; Exodus 30:12–16; Numbers 14:41; Genesis 4:10; Luke 11:49–51; Matthew 23:34–36; Acts 7:58–60; Hebrews 11:37

settings.what: Joash's orders for the Temple tax
settings.to: The priests and Levites; then Jehoiada the head priest; then all Judah and Jerusalem by proclamation
settings.when: After it came into Joash's heart to renew the LORD's house
settings.why: The same scene as 2 Kings 12:4–8, but Chronicles calls the money 'Moses' tax,' the half-shekel of Exodus 30:12–16. It sets the chest outside the gate where all the people bring their gifts with joy. Kings tells a story about honest accounting. Chronicles tells about a whole people giving by Moses' law, which was the readers' own practice (Nehemiah 10:32).

settings.by: Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest, clothed by God's Spirit
settings.to: The people of Judah, in the courtyard of the LORD's house
settings.when: After Jehoiada's death, when the leaders turned to Asherah poles and idols
settings.why: 'Why are you going against the LORD's commands?... You have left the LORD, so he has left you.' The oracle states the book's rule in a sentence. The people stone him on the king's order. For readers it named the cost of rejecting God's messengers, and Jesus later recalled 'the blood of Zechariah' (Luke 11:51).

settings.to: The LORD, as he died
settings.when: As he was stoned in the Temple court
settings.why: 'May the LORD see it, and may he seek it out.' A cry for justice, answered within a year (24:23–25). Rabbinic tradition told of his blood seething until the Babylonian conquest (Bavli Gittin 57b), and readers took it as a warning that innocent blood is not forgotten.
